Department of Renal and Body Fluid Physiology, Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences Warsaw Poland ([ROR:05d3ntb42](https://ror.org/05d3ntb42)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract Rats are believed to communicate their emotional state by emitting two distinct types of ultrasonic vocalizations. The first is long ‘22-kHz’ vocalizations (>300 ms, <32-kHz) with constant frequency, signaling aversive states, and the second is short ‘50-kHz’ calls (<150 ms, >32 kHz), often frequency-modulated, in appetitive situations. Here, we describe aversive vocalizations emitted at a higher pitch by male Wistar and spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) in an intensified aversive state – prolonged fear conditioning. These calls, which we named ‘44-kHz’ vocalizations, are long (>150 ms), generally at a constant frequency (usually within 35–50-kHz range) and have an overall spectrographic image similar to 22-kHz calls. Some 44-kHz vocalizations are comprised of both 22-kHz-like and 44-kHz-like elements. Furthermore, two separate clustering methods confirmed that these 44-kHz calls can be separated from other vocalizations. We observed 44-kHz calls to be associated with freezing behavior during fear conditioning training, during which they constituted up to 19.4% of all calls and most of them appeared next to each other forming uniform groups of vocalizations (bouts). We also show that some of rats’ responses to the playback of 44-kHz calls were more akin to that of aversive calls, for example, heart rate changes, whereas other responses were at an intermediate level between aversive and appetitive calls. Our results suggest that rats have a wider vocal repertoire than previously believed, and current definitions of major call types may require reevaluation. We hope that future investigations of 44-kHz calls in rat models of human diseases will contribute to expanding our understanding and therapeutic strategies related to human psychiatric conditions. ## Introduction Charles Darwin wrote: “That the pitch of the voice bears some relation to certain states of feeling is tolerably clear” (Darwin, 1872). This has also been tolerably clearly observed and widely described for ultrasonic vocalizations of rats (Brudzynski, 2019; Brudzynski, 2021; Simola and Granon, 2019) which emit low-pitched aversive calls and high-pitched appetitive calls. The former are ‘22-kHz’ vocalizations (Figures 1A and 2A), with 18–32 kHz frequency range, monotonous and long, usually >300 ms, and are uttered in distress (Brudzynski, 2013; Brudzynski, 2019; Brudzynski, 2021; Simola and Granon, 2019). The latter are ‘50-kHz’ vocalizations (Figure 1C), are relatively short (10–150 ms), frequency-modulated, usually within 35–80 kHz, and they signal appetitive and rewarding states (Simola and Granon, 2019; Brudzynski, 2013; Brudzynski, 2019; Brudzynski, 2021). Therefore, these two types of calls communicate the animal’s emotional state to their social group (Brudzynski, 2013). Low-pitch (<32 kHz), short (<300 ms; Figure 1B) calls, assumed to also express a negative aversive state, have been described but their role is not clearly established (Brudzynski, 2013). Notably, high-pitch (>32 kHz), long and monotonous ultrasonic vocalizations have not yet been described. Here, we show these unmodulated rat vocalizations with peak frequency (i.e., peak frequency of a given vocalization is defined here as the highest power peak in the averaged spectrum of the entire element) at about 44 kHz (Figure 1B and E; Figure 2B), emitted in aversive experimental situations, especially in prolonged fear conditioning. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/88810/elife-88810-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 1.:** (A) Some rats produced aversive 22-kHz vocalizations with typical features, that is, constant-frequency of <32 kHz, >300 ms duration – both values marked as dotted lines); example emission from one rat. These vocalizations, for example, top-right group in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, were outside the defined range (Brudzynski, 2019; Brudzynski, 2021; Simola and Granon, 2019) for both 50-kHz (bottom-right group in Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C) and 22-kHz calls (top-left group in Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C). These vocalizations were also observed in a different rat strain acquired from a different breeding colony, that is, spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) (Brudzynski, 2021; Okamoto and Aoki, 1963), also trained in delay fear conditioning (Table 1/Exp. 2/#10–12; Olszyński et al., 2023). In particular, 6 of the 49 conditioned SHR displayed high-pitch, long, monotonous vocalizations (e.g., Figure 2—figure supplement 1G); moreover, we observed more of these vocalizations in Wistar rats compared to SHR (Table 1/Exp. 2/#6–8,10–12) in both training, p<0.0001, and test sessions, p=0.0030, Mann–Whitney. **Table 1.** All fear conditioning (FC) experiments described in the text.

_*Control groups._ Overall, we analyzed 140,149 vocalizations from all fear conditioning experiments (Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#1–13, n = 218) and through trial-and-error, we set new criteria, namely peak frequency of >32 kHz and >150 ms duration to define the calls described above. We manually verified the results on the spectrogram using these parameters and only 308 calls (0.2%) were incorrectly assigned (i.e., exceptionally long 50-kHz vocalizations misplaced in the newly defined group or borderline-short vocalizations of the newly defined group misplaced to 50-kHz calls). Hence, the new parameters correctly assigned 99.8% of cases and are thus effective to distinguish the newly defined calls in an automated fashion. Finally, 10,445 newly defined calls were identified, which constituted 7.5% of the total calls during fear conditioning experiments (Table 1/Exp. 1–3; comp. Figure 1G). These vocalizations have a peak frequency range from 32.2 to 51.5 kHz (95% of cases) with an average peak frequency of 42.1 kHz, and they exhibited 43.8 kHz peak frequency at the cluster center in a DBSCAN analysis (Figure 3A). In line with the accepted nomenclature convention, underlining the relationship with 22-kHz vocalizations, we christened this newly defined calls as ‘44-kHz vocalizations’. ![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/88810/elife-88810-fig3-v1.jpg) **Figure 3.:** (A) DBSCAN algorithm (ε = 0.14) clustering of vocalizations from all fear conditioning experiments (Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#1–13, n = 218), silhouette coefficient = 0.198, two clusters emerge, cluster of green dots n = 77,243 (due to high generality of cluster average peak frequency and duration deemed redundant), cluster of red dots n = 5,646 (average peak frequency = 43,826.6 Hz, average duration = 0.524 s), some calls were not assigned to any cluster, that is, outlier vocalizations, black dots, n = 4,139. When we analyzed all Wistar rats that had undergone 10 trials of fear conditioning (Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,8,13; n = 46), these vocalizations were less frequent following the first trial (1.2 ± 0.4% of all calls), and increased in subsequent trials, particularly after the 5th (8.8 ± 2.8%), through the 9th (19.4 ± 5.5%, the highest value), to the 10th (15.5 ± 4.9%) trials, where 44-kHz calls gradually replaced 22-kHz vocalizations in some rats (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B, Figure 1—video 1; comp. Figure 1D vs. Figure 1E). Please note that the majority of the 22-kHz calls were emitted after the 3rd shock, that is, during the 3rd inter-trial interval (ITI), while 44-kHz vocalizations were emitted in the second part of the training, that is, 5th to 10th ITI (Figure 1F, comp. Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B). From this group of rats (n = 46), n = 41 (89.1%) emitted long 22-kHz calls, and 32 of them (69.6%) emitted 44-kHz calls, that is, every animal that produced 44-kHz calls also emitted long 22-kHz calls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B). The prevalence of 44-kHz calls varied greatly among individual rats, such that for n = 3 rats, 44-kHz vocalizations accounted for >95% of all calls during at least one ITI (e.g., 140 of total 142, 222 of 231, and 263 of 265 tallied 44-kHz calls), and in n = 9 rats, 44-kHz vocalizations constituted >50% of calls in more than one ITI. The prevalence of 44-kHz calls in all experimental conditions analyzed in all animal groups is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3. Notably, there were more 44-kHz vocalizations during fear conditioning training than testing in all fear-conditioned Wistar rats (Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,6–8,13; n = 84; 3.63 ± 0.99 vs. 0.23 ± 0.13 calls/min; p<0.0001; Wilcoxon). In a recent publication during this paper’s review process, Gonzalez-Palomares et al., 2023, in line with the findings reported here, investigated and described 44-kHz vocalizations following prolonged (10-trial protocol) odor fear conditioning. These calls were observed predominantly during the late ITI, that is, 8th–10th ITI (Gonzalez-Palomares et al., 2023; Fig. S4C; please note 4th–7th ITI were not investigated) after the shock presentations (Fig. S4B therein), which complement our results. ### Changes in frequency, duration, and mean power of long aversive calls during conditioning Analyzing Wistar rats that had undergone 10 trials of fear conditioning (Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,8,13; n = 46), we also observed the frequencies of 22-kHz calls to gradually rise throughout fear conditioning training, that is, during subsequent ITI – from 24.5 ± 0.1 to 27.9 ± 0.4 kHz (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; p<0.0001, Friedman, p=0.0039, Wilcoxon). The frequency levels of 44-kHz vocalizations also appeared to rise – from 37.8 ± 2.1 to 39.6 ± 1.3 kHz (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) but we were unable to statistically demonstrate it (p=0.0155, Friedman, p=0.0977, Wilcoxon). There was a shortening of long 22-kHz calls during the first four ITI from 969.6 ± 43.1 ms to 794.6 ± 39.8 ms (p<0.0001, Friedman; p<0.0001, Wilcoxon, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), while 44-kHz vocalizations were longest during the 4th ITI (the time of their substantial appearance, comp. Figure 1F), that is, 775.0 ± 135.7 ms, and shortened over subsequent ITI (619.6 ± 58.1 ms for the 10th ITI, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, p=0.0227, Friedman; p=0.0234, Wilcoxon). Finally, the sound mean power of 44-kHz vocalizations appeared to remain stable throughout the 10-trial sessions, while during the first half of the training, that is, 1st–5th ITI, 22-kHz calls were not only significantly more frequent but also louder than during the second half, that is, 6th–10th ITI (p<0.0001, Wilcoxon). Consequently, long 22-kHz calls appeared louder than 44-kHz calls (p=0.0397–0.0038, Mann–Whitney). However, in the second half of the session, this difference dissipated due to the diminishing amplitude of 22-kHz vocalizations (p=0.0083, Friedman; p=0.0046, Wilcoxon), while the amplitude of 44-kHz calls remained stable (p=0.0663, Friedman; p=0.2661, Wilcoxon; 6th ITI through 10th ITI for both; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E). After adjusting for angle-dependent hardware attenuation (see ‘Materials and methods’, ‘Sound mean power’), the situation reversed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F). Both long 22-kHz and 44-kHz vocalizations showed similar amplitude levels during the first half of the fear conditioning training session, while during the 6th–10th ITI, 44-kHz calls were significantly louder than long 22-kHz calls (p=0.0007–0.0097, Mann–Whitney). ### 44-kHz calls linked to freezing We investigated the freezing behavior of all Wistar rats emitting 44-kHz vocalizations during 10 trials of fear conditioning training (Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,8,13; n = 46). The training sessions were divided into 10-s-long time bins, from which we analyzed only the bins that had exclusively long 22-kHz or 44-kHz calls. For comparison, we also measured the freezing levels during the first 5 min of the trial (baseline freezing levels before any foot-shocks) as well as the bins in which animals did not vocalize (from the period after the first shock to the end of the session). Of the n = 46 rats analyzed, n = 41 emitted 22-kHz vocalizations, from which n = 32 also emitted 44-kHz vocalizations, from which only n = 21 were determined to have both – 10-s-long bins of 22-kHz calls only and 44-kHz calls only (Table 2A). Freezing during the bins of 22-kHz calls only (p<0.0001, for both groups) and during 44-kHz calls only bins (p=0.0003) was higher than during the first 5 min baseline freezing levels of the session. Also, the freezing associated with emissions of 44-kHz calls only was higher than during bins with no ultrasonic vocalizations (p=0.0353), and it was also 9.9 percentage points higher than during time bins with only long 22-kHz vocalizations, but the difference was not significant (p=0.1907; all Wilcoxon). **Table 2.** Freezing associated with emission of long, monotonous vocalizations.All Wistar rats that had undergone 10 trials of fear conditioning training were analyzed (Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,8,13; n = 46). The minimal freezing behavior detection window was reduced to compensate for the higher resolution of the measurements (3, 5, 10, or 15 video frames were used). There was no difference in freezing during the emission of 44-kHz vs. 22-kHz vocalizations for ≥150-ms-long calls (3 frames, p=0.2054) and for ≥500-ms-long calls (5 frames, p=0.2404; 10 frames, p=0.4498; 15 frames, p=0.7776; all Wilcoxon, Table 2B). ### 44-kHz calls sorted into five subtypes While the majority of 44-kHz vocalizations were of continuous unmodulated frequency (Figure 2B), some comprised additional elements. Based on the composition of individual call elements and their relation to each other, we manually sorted the calls into five categories (Figure 2B–F). If the start (prefix) or end (suffix) portion of a call was less than 1/5th the length of the following or previous element, this portion of the call was not considered in its categorization into the five subtypes. The names and descriptions of the five subtypes are: flat – single element with near constant frequency and little to no interruptions to the sound continuity on the spectrogram; step up – two elements with an instantaneous frequency jump, where the first element is of lower frequency; step down – two elements with an instantaneous frequency jump, where the first element is of higher frequency; insert – three elements with an instantaneous frequency change, where the middle element is of different frequency; and complex – more than three elements with instantaneous frequency changes. ### 44-kHz and 22-kHz calls closely related 44-kHz were emitted in aversive behavioral situations – as 22-kHz calls are observed (Antoniadis and McDonald, 1999; Dupin et al., 2019; Taylor et al., 2017). Both types of calls are long (usually >300 ms) and frequency-unmodulated. Some of the elements constituting such as step up; step down; insert and complex 44-kHz vocalizations (Figure 2C–F) were at a lower frequency – typical for 22-kHz vocalizations. Vice versa we also observed 22-kHz calls with 44-kHz-like elements. Therefore, we propose that these long 22-kHz and 44-kHz vocalizations constitute a supertype group of long unmodulated aversive calls (‘long 22/44-kHz vocalizations’). We observed a stable, approximately 1.5 ratio in peak frequency levels between 22-kHz and 44-kHz vocalizations within individual rats. Specifically, in 14 rats (13 Wistar and 1 SHR) with a clear transition from 22-kHz to 44-kHz calls during the fear conditioning training session (n = 14, selected from Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,6–8,10–13), the proportion between the frequencies of the long 22-kHz vocalizations and the long 44-kHz calls was 1.48 ± 0.02. Similar results were obtained for 70 step up (1.53 ± 0.03) and 65 step down (1.59 ± 0.02) 44-kHz calls – altogether suggesting a 1.5 times or 3:2 frequency ratio. This ratio and its relevance have been observed in invertebrates and vertebrates including human speech and music (Hoeschele, 2017). In music theory, 3:2 frequency ratio is referred to as a perfect fifth and is often featured, for example, the first two notes of the Star Wars 1977 movie (ascending, i.e., step up; comp. Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1) and Game of Thrones 2011 television series (descending, i.e., step down; comp. Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 2) theme songs. All of these may point to a common basis for this sound interval and its prevalence that could be explained by the observation that all physical objects capable of producing tonal sounds generate harmonic vibrations, the most prominent being the octave, perfect fifth, and major third (Christensen, 1993, discussed in Bowling and Purves, 2015). ### 44-kHz calls separated in cluster analyses Next, we showed that 44-kHz calls indeed constitute a separable type of ultrasonic vocalizations as it was sorted into isolated clusters by two different methods. First, using the DBSCAN algorithm method based on calls’ peak frequency and duration, we were able to divide all vocalizations recorded during all training sessions into 44-kHz vocalizations vs. all other vocalizations as two separate clusters (Figure 3A). Secondly, a clustering algorithm that includes call contours, that is, k-means with UMAP done via DeepSqueak (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), sorted 44-kHz vocalizations of different subtypes including unusual ones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F), into topologically-separate groups. Notably, flat 44-kHz calls were consistently in a separate cluster from 22-kHz calls (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). ### 44-kHz calls formed separate groups We have examined transition probabilities for call-type transitions within all vocalizations and within vocalization bouts in all Wistar rats during 10 trials of fear conditioning training (Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,8,13; n = 46). Transition probabilities between vocalization types were defined by counting the number of specific pair sequences and dividing by all observed sequence pairs where the first type of signal is followed by any signal. The most probable call following long 22-kHz vocalization was another long 22-kHz vocalization (94.4% probability). Similarly, the most probable call following 44-kHz vocalization was another 44-kHz call (83.1%). These values augmented when the analysis was limited to vocalizations emitted only in bouts, that is, with <320 ms time gaps between calls (Wöhr et al., 2005), and reached 96.3 and 86.5%, respectively. Examples of parts of groups of both types of calls are demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. ### Response to 44-kHz playback To describe the behavioral and physiological impact of 44-kHz vocalizations, we performed playback experiments in two separate groups of rats (‘Materials and methods’, Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Values are means ± SEM. ## Discussion As Charles Darwin noted above (Darwin, 1872) and other researchers have confirmed (Briefer et al., 2012), the frequency level of animal calls is a vocal parameter that changes in accordance with its arousal state (intensity) or emotional valence (positive/negative state). The frequency shifts toward both higher and lower levels, that is, alterations were observed during both positive (appetitive) and negative (agonistic/aversive) situations; however, as a general rule, frequency usually increases with an increase in arousal (Briefer et al., 2012). We would like to propose a hypothesis that our prolonged fear conditioning increased the arousal of the rats with no change in the valence of the aversive stimuli. It could also be speculated that several other factors, apart from increased arousal, contributed to the emergence of 44-kHz vocalizations in our fear-conditioned rats, for example, heightened fear, stress/anxiety, annoyance/anger, disgust/boredom, grief/sadness, despair/helplessness, and weariness/fatigue. It is not possible, at this stage, to definitively determine which factors played a decisive role. Please note that the potential contribution of these factors is not mutually exclusive. However, several arguments support the idea that 44-kHz vocalizations communicate an increased negative emotional state. First, in general, ultrasonic vocalizations serve as a means of communicating rats’ emotional state (Brudzynski, 2013). Second, the changing of the pitch of the voice bears some relation to certain states of feeling (Darwin, 1872). Third, 44-kHz calls were notably more frequent during prolonged aversive stimulation, that is, the 5th–10th trials of fear conditioning training. Fourth, they were linked to freezing. Fifth, they appeared as partial replacements of, established as aversive, 22-kHz calls – in the presence of the same painful stimulus. Sixth, numerous instances of vocalizations featured both 22-kHz-like and 44-kHz-like call elements. Also, several observations contradict the potential contribution of fatigue. The sound mean power of 44-kHz vocalizations was comparable to, or possibly even higher than, that of 22-kHz calls, despite the higher energy costs associated with producing higher-pitched calls (Sonninen and Hurme, 1998), that is, the rats emitting 44-kHz calls invested additional energy to communicate their emotional state; both in vivo measurements (Riede, 2013) and computer modeling (Håkansson et al., 2022) demonstrated that producing calls of higher frequency, such as 50-kHz vs. 22-kHz, requires increased activity of various muscles. Additionally, the mean power of 44-kHz vocalizations remained strong and stable for several trials – in contrast to 22-kHz vocalizations. Finally, when 44-kHz calls started to appear in significant numbers, that is, after the 4th–5th trials of fear conditioning training, they were as long as 22-kHz vocalizations. Concerning the latter, we observed a significant decrease in the mean power of 22-kHz vocalizations during the fear conditioning training session. Such reduction could potentially be attributed to fatigue (as observed in humans, Kitch and Oates, 1994), despair (e.g., as a reaction to the lack of effects from repeated emissions of 22-kHz calls), or both. The reduction in the amplitude of 22-kHz calls during the 10-trial fear conditioning training was also recently observed by others (Gonzalez-Palomares et al., 2023). Importantly, it has been demonstrated multiple times that training rats with several electric foot-shocks (i.e., 5–10 shocks) produces a qualitatively different kind of fear memory compared to training with only 1–2 shocks. Training with more numerous shocks has been shown to result in augmented freezing (e.g., Fanselow and Bolles, 1979; Haubrich et al., 2020; Haubrich and Nader, 2023; Poulos et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2009), which reflects a more intense fear memory that is resistant to extinction (Haubrich et al., 2020; Haubrich and Nader, 2023), resistant to reconsolidation blockade (Haubrich et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2009; Finnie and Nader, 2020), associated with downregulation of NR2B NMDA-receptor subunits as well as elevated amyloid-beta concentrations in the lateral and basal amygdala (Finnie and Nader, 2020; Wang et al., 2009). Additionally, it involves activation of the noradrenaline-locus coeruleus system (Haubrich et al., 2020) and collective changes in connectivity across multiple brain regions within the neural network (Haubrich and Nader, 2023). Notably, it has also been shown that higher freezing as a result of fear conditioning training correlates with increased concentrations of stress hormone, corticosterone, in the blood (Dos Santos Corrêa et al., 2019). The rats subjected to 6- and 10-trial fear conditioning training, whose results are reported herein (Table 1/Exp. 2/#7,8,11,12; n = 73), also demonstrated higher freezing than rats subjected to 1-trial conditioning (Table 1/Exp. 2/#6,10; n = 33), which is reported elsewhere (Olszyński et al., 2021, Fig. S1C–E; Olszyński et al., 2023, Fig. S1D–G). Therefore, we postulate that emission of 44-kHz calls is associated with increased stress and the training regime forming robust memories. Amounting research points to the utility of rat ultrasonic vocalizations to alter emotional states, evidenced by behavioral changes, in tested rats via playback of affectively valenced calls (Bonauto et al., 2023). We have exposed rats to 44-kHz playback along with 22-kHz and 50-kHz playback. The experimental design (see ‘Materials and methods’ for details) allowed us to compare rats’ responses to 22-kHz vs. 44-kHz playbacks, especially with 50-kHz playback used as a form of control or baseline. In general, the rats responded similarly to hearing 44-kHz calls as they did to hearing aversive 22-kHz calls, especially regarding heart rate change, despite the 44-kHz calls occupying the frequency band of appetitive 50-kHz vocalizations. This is contrary to some observations (Saito et al., 2019), which suggested that frequency band plays the main role in rat ultrasound perception. Please factor in potential carry-over effects (resulting from hearing playbacks of the same valence in a row) in the differences between responses to 50-kHz vs. 22/44-kHz playbacks, especially those observed before the signal (Figure 4A and B). Other responses to 44-kHz calls were intermediate, they fell between response levels to appetitive vs. aversive playback, which might signify some behavioral specificity and importance (or possibly confusion). These latter effects were similar in both playback experiments despite an array of methodological differences between them. Overall, these initial results raise further questions about how, ethologically, animals may interpret the variation in hearing 22-kHz vs. 44-kHz calls and integrate this interpretation in their responses. The question also is, why have the 44-kHz vocalizations been overlooked until now? On one hand, long (or not that long as in Bialy et al., 2019), frequency-stable high-pitch vocalizations have been reported before (e.g., Sales, 1979; Shimoju et al., 2020), notably as caused by intense cholinergic stimulation (Brudzynski and Bihari, 1990) or higher shock-dose fear conditioning (Wöhr et al., 2005). However, they have not been systematically defined, described, fully shown, or demonstrated to be a separate type of vocalization. On the other hand, 44-kHz calls were likely omitted as the analyses were restricted to canonical groups, that is, flat 22-kHz and short 50-kHz calls, with a sharp dividing frequency border between the two (e.g., Kalamari et al., 2021; Potasiewicz et al., 2020; Turner et al., 2019) or even a frequency ‘safety gap’ between 22-kHz and 50-kHz vocalizations (e.g., Silkstone and Brudzynski, 2019; Garcia et al., 2015). Moreover, many older bat detectors had limited frequency-range detection (e.g., up to 40-kHz in Sales, 1991) when stress-evoked types of ultrasonic calls were being established. Finally, 44-kHz vocalizations are emitted much fewer than 22-kHz calls (Figure 1F and G). Here, we present introductory evidence that 44-kHz vocalizations are a separate and behaviorally relevant group of rat ultrasonic calls. These results require further confirmations and additional experiments, also in form of replication, including research on female rat subjects. However, our results bring to awareness that rats employ these previously unrecognized, long, high-pitched and flat aversive calls in their vocal repertoire. Researchers investigating rat ultrasonic vocalizations should be aware of their potential presence and to not rely fully on automated detection of high- vs. low-pitch calls. ## Materials and methods **Key resources table**

### Animals Wistar rats (n = 167) were obtained from The Center for Experimental Medicine of the Medical University of Białystok, Poland; SHR (n = 80) and Sprague–Dawley rats (n = 16) were from Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences, Poland. All the details are described in Olszyński et al., 2021 and Olszyński et al., 2023. #### Delay fear conditioning experiment, rats without transmitters Wistar rats were housed in pairs; were not implanted with radiotelemetric transmitters to eliminate the potential effect of surgical intervention on vocalization; they received 10 conditioning stimuli at 12 weeks of age (Table 1/Exp. 3/#13, n = 10) – the same as in Olszyński et al., 2021 and Olszyński et al., 2023. #### Playback experiment, rats with transmitters Wistar rats (n = 29) were housed in pairs; all were implanted with a radiotelemetric transmitter 1 week before the playback experiment. At 12 weeks of age, one group (n = 13) heard 50-kHz appetitive vocalization playback while the other (n = 16) 22-kHz and 44-kHz aversive calls (for details, see below). #### Playback experiment, rats without transmitters Sprague–Dawley rats (n = 15) were housed in pairs, were not implanted with the transmitters, and received 22-kHz, 44-kHz, and 50-kHz ultrasonic vocalization playback at 8 weeks of age (see below). ### Surgery, transmitter implantation, and heart rate registration Radiotelemetric transmitters (HD-S10, Data Sciences International, St. Paul, MN) were implanted into the abdominal aorta of rats in specified groups as previously described (Olszyński et al., 2020; Olszyński et al., 2021). An illustrative image with the surgery details can be found elsewhere (Figure 5 in Pestana-Oliveira et al., 2020; please note that tissue glue was used instead of cellulose patches and silk sutures). Readings were processed using Dataquest ART (version 4.36, Data Sciences International) for trace fear conditioning (Table 1/Exp. 1) and Ponemah (version 6.32, Data Sciences International) software for other experiments Table 1/Exp. 2–3 and playback experiments. ### Fear conditioning All conditioning procedures were conducted in a chamber (VFC-008-LP, Med Associates, Fairfax, VT) located in an outer cubicle (MED-VFC2-USB-R, Med Associates) equipped with an ultrasound CM16/CMPA condenser microphone (Avisoft Bioacoustics, Berlin, Germany). Ultrasonic vocalizations were recorded via Avisoft USGH Recorder (Avisoft Bioacoustics), and rat behavior was recorded via NIR monochrome camera (VID-CAM-MONO-6, Med Associates). All procedures were described in detail before (Olszyński et al., 2021; Olszyński et al., 2023). #### Trace fear conditioning Trace fear conditioning (Table 1/Exp. 1/#1–4, n = 34 rats) was performed similarly to some previous reports (e.g., Jaholkowski et al., 2009). Rats were individually placed in the fear conditioning apparatus in one of two different contexts: A (safe) or B (unsafe). Context A was in an illuminated room with the cage interior with white light, the cage floor was made of solid plastic, and the cage was scented with lemon odor, cleaned with a 10% ethanol solution; the experimenter was male wearing white gloves. Context B was a different, dark room, with the cage interior with green light, the floor was made of metal bars, and the cage was scented with mint odor, cleaned with 1% acetic acid; the experimenter was female with violet gloves. The procedure: on day –2, each rat was habituated to context A for 20 min; on day –1, habituated to context B for 20 min; on day 0, each rat was placed for 52 min in context A; on day 1, after 10 min in context B, the rat received 10 conditioning stimuli (15-s-long sine wave tone, 5-kHz, 85 dB) followed by a 30 s trace period and a foot-shock (1 s, 1 mA) and 210 s ITI; total session duration: 52 min. Control rats were subjected to the same procedures but did not receive the electric shock at the end of trace periods. These two groups were therefore reported together. ### Measuring freezing Freezing behavior was scored automatically using Video Freeze software (Med Associates) with a default motion index threshold of 18. To avoid including brief moments of the animal’s stillness, freezing was measured only if the animal did not move for at least 1 s, that is, 30 video frames, with some exceptions, see next. #### Vocalization-nested freezing behavior Freezing at the exact times of ultrasonic calling was measured in rats that had undergone 10 trials of fear conditioning training, which produced 44-kHz calls (n = 32, selected from Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,8,13). From each rat, one 44-kHz call was randomly selected along with the long 22-kHz call closest to it. Such pairs of vocalizations were selected with either ≥150 ms duration (n = 32) or ≥500 ms duration (n = 28). For each pair of vocalizations, the freezing behavior was calculated from the entire duration of the shorter call and for the equal-time-length period in the middle of the longer vocalization. The sound interval was adjusted if it was peculiarly long or the sequence was interrupted by other types of calls in the original recordings. #### Playback procedure, rats with transmitters As previously described (Olszyński et al., 2020; Olszyński et al., 2021; Olszyński et al., 2023). Since initial analysis showed no differences within responses to 22-kHz aversive sets and within responses to 50-kHz appetitive sets, we decided to show the results following playback of 44-kHz long calls (set no. 1), 22-kHz long calls (set no. 2), and 50-kHz modulated calls (set no. 5) only. #### Playback procedure, rats without transmitters Before playback presentation, animals were habituated for 3 min to the experimental conditions, that is, recording cage, presence of the speaker and microphone, over 4 days. Proximity to the speaker was expressed as the percentage of time spent in the half of the cage closer to the ultrasonic speaker. The center point of each animal’s shape was used as a reference point for measurements of locomotor activity, thus registering only full-body movements. ### Analysis of ultrasonic vocalizations Audio recordings were analyzed manually using SASLab Pro (version 5.2.xx, Avisoft Bioacoustics) as described (Dupin et al., 2019; Olszyński et al., 2020; Olszyński et al., 2021; Olszyński et al., 2023) to measure key features of calls and categorize them into subtypes. ### Sound mean power This was measured as the average spectra power density of the vocalization contour using DeepSqueak software. Initially, calls were detected using the default rat long-vocalization neural network (Long Rat Detector YOLO R1) and subsequently manually reviewed and corrected where necessary. We analyzed a subset of Wistar rats subjected to 10-trial fear conditioning training that emitted more than 20 instances of 44-kHz calls during the fear conditioning training session (n = 17, selected from Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,8,13). It is important to note that due to the directional characteristics of the microphones used, angular attenuation occurred during audio recording. This phenomenon results in a selective reduction in the intensity of higher frequency sounds, dependent on the angle between the sound emitter and the microphone (as specified in the CM16/CMPA microphone hardware specification page, Avisoft Bioacoustics, 2023). In our experimental setup, we approximated a 45° angle between the plane of the rat’s head and the plane of the microphone’s membrane. This angle corresponds to an estimated 10 dB attenuation (adopting a conservative estimate) of 40-kHz frequencies compared to 20-kHz frequencies for which there is even a small dB gain due to these hardware properties, 44-kHz calls are predicted to be approximately at least 10 dB louder in reality than what was recorded. #### 22-kHz vs. 44-kHz frequency ratio A clear transition between 22-kHz and 44-kHz long calls was observed in n = 13 Wistar rats and n = 1 SHR. In each case, ten 22-kHz calls followed by ten 44-kHz calls were analyzed (n = 14, selected from Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,6–8,10–13). #### Step up and step down frequency ratio Rats that emitted at least five vocalizations of the specific subtype were analyzed (step up, n = 14; step down, n = 13; selected from Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,7,8,13); five calls of the two subtypes from each rat were chosen randomly and the frequencies of their elements were measured. #### Ultrasonic vocalizations clustering (two independent methods) Calls of conditioned and control animals were taken from all fear conditioning training sessions (Table 1/Exp. 1–3, n = 218). We used DBSCAN algorithm (Ester et al., 1996), a density based method, from the scikit-learn (sklearn) Python package, because of its ability to detect a desired number of clusters of arbitrary shape; with two main input parameters: MinPts (minimal number of points forming the core of the cluster) and ε (the maximum distance two points can be from one another while still belonging to the same cluster). To avoid detecting small clusters, we limited MinPts to 150 samples. The heuristic method described by Ester et al., 1996 was implemented to find the initial range of ε. All the input data were standardized. The silhouette coefficient (Rousseeuw, 1987) was used to control the quality of the clustering. Maximizing ε among different ranges helped to select the most relevant number of identified clusters. Clustering with ε in the range of 0.14–0.2 resulted in a silhouette coefficient around 0.2–0.5. #### k-means algorithm Vocalizations of selected fear-conditioned rats with 6–10 shocks and >30 of 44-kHz calls (n = 26, selected from Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,7,8,11–13) were detected using a built-in neural network for long rat calls (Long Rat Detector YOLO R1) on DeepSqueak (Coffey et al., 2019) software (version 3.0.4) running under MATLAB (version 2021b, MathWorks, Natick, MA) and manually revised for missed and mismatched calls. Unsupervised k-means clustering was based on call contour, frequency and duration variables, with equal weights assigned, and several descending elbow optimization parameters were used to obtain different maximum numbers of clusters together with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction (UMAP) (McInnes et al., 2018) for superimposing and visualization of clusters. ### Quantification and statistical analysis Data were analyzed using non-parametric Friedman, Wilcoxon, Mann–Whitney tests with GraphPad Prism 8.4.3 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA); the p values are given, p<0.05 as the minimal level of significance. In particular, the Friedman test was used to assess the presence of change within the sequence of several ITI, while the Wilcoxon test was used for the difference between the first and the last ITI analyzed. Figures were prepared using the same software and depict average values with a standard error of the mean (SEM).

Olszyński et al. claim that they identified a "new-type" ultrasonic vocalization around 44 kHz that occurs in response to prolonged fear conditioning (using foot-shocks of relatively high intensity, i.e. 1 mA) in rats. Typically, negative 22-kHz calls and positive 50-kHz calls are distinguished in rats, commonly by using a frequency threshold of 30 or 32 kHz. Olszyński et al. now observed so-called "44-kHz" calls in a substantial number of subjects exposed to 10 tone-shock pairings, yet call emission rate was low (according to Fig. 1G around 15%, according to the result text around 7.5%). They also performed playback experiments and concluded that "the responses to 44-kHz aversive calls presented from the speaker were either similar to 22-kHz vocalizations or in-between responses to 22-kHz and 50-kHz playbacks".

Strengths: Detailed spectrographic analysis of a substantial data set of ultrasonic vocalizations recorded during prolonged fear conditioning, combined with playback experiments.

claims.claim: 44-kHz vocalizations can be sorted into five subtypes: flat, step up, step down, insert, and complex.
claims.source: Based on the composition of individual call elements and their relation to each other, we manually sorted the calls into five categories (Figure 2B–F). If the start (prefix) or end (suffix) portion of a call was less than 1/5th the length of the following or previous element, this portion of the call was not considered in its categorization into the five subtypes. The names and descriptions of the five subtypes are: flat – single element with near constant frequency and little to no interruptions to the sound continuity on the spectrogram; step up – two elements with an instantaneous frequency jump, where the first element is of lower frequency; step down – two elements with an instantaneous frequency jump, where the first element is of higher frequency; insert – three elements with an instantaneous frequency change, where the middle element is of different frequency; and complex – more than three elements with instantaneous frequency changes.

results.result: Male Wistar rats and spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) emit 44-kHz ultrasonic vocalizations during prolonged fear conditioning, with 53 of 84 Wistar rats and 6 of 49 SHR displaying these calls. Wistar rats emitted significantly more 44-kHz vocalizations than SHR in both training and test sessions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C31-C33 provide clear quantitative evidence from three separate experiments showing that both rat strains emit 44-kHz vocalizations during fear conditioning, with statistical comparisons between strains. The data are well-documented with specific sample sizes and p-values.

results.result: 44-kHz vocalizations are characterized by duration >150 ms, constant frequency typically within 35-50 kHz range (95% of cases: 32.2-51.5 kHz), average peak frequency of 42.1 kHz, and spectrographic similarity to 22-kHz calls. Classification criteria of >32 kHz peak frequency and >150 ms duration correctly identified 99.8% of 10,445 44-kHz calls (7.5% of total vocalizations).
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6 and C35-C39 provide detailed acoustic characterization with quantitative measurements and validation. The 99.8% classification accuracy (C35) demonstrates robust criteria, though the trial-and-error approach to setting thresholds could introduce some circularity. The large sample size (140,149 total vocalizations) strengthens the findings.

results.result: 44-kHz vocalizations can be classified into five subtypes (flat, step up, step down, insert, and complex) based on frequency composition, with some calls containing both 22-kHz-like and 44-kHz-like elements, and vice versa.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C71, C74-C75 describe structural heterogeneity within 44-kHz calls with clear classification criteria. The manual sorting approach is appropriate for this descriptive analysis, though inter-rater reliability is not reported. The observation of mixed elements supports the proposed relationship between call types.

results.result: 44-kHz vocalizations emerge progressively during 10-trial fear conditioning, increasing from 1.2±0.4% after trial 1 to peak at 19.4±5.5% after trial 9, predominantly appearing in the second half of training (5th-10th ITI). 69.6% of rats (32/46) emitted 44-kHz calls, and every rat producing 44-kHz calls also emitted 22-kHz calls.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C50 provide detailed temporal dynamics with quantitative data and appropriate statistics. The progressive emergence pattern is well-documented, though individual variability is high (C49-C50). The universal co-occurrence with 22-kHz calls (C48) is a strong finding supporting the relationship between call types.

results.result: 44-kHz vocalizations were significantly more frequent during fear conditioning training than testing (3.63±0.99 vs 0.23±0.13 calls/min, p<0.0001). Independent confirmation from Gonzalez-Palomares et al., 2023 showed similar calls during late ITI (8th-10th) in odor fear conditioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 demonstrate context-specificity with strong statistical support and independent replication. The convergent evidence from a different laboratory using a different conditioning paradigm (odor vs. shock) strengthens the validity of the findings.

results.result: During 10-trial fear conditioning, 22-kHz call frequency increased significantly from 24.5±0.1 to 27.9±0.4 kHz (p<0.0001), while 44-kHz frequency showed a non-significant trend from 37.8±2.1 to 39.6±1.3 kHz (p=0.0977). Call durations changed over trials: 22-kHz calls shortened from 969.6±43.1 to 794.6±39.8 ms, while 44-kHz calls peaked at 775.0±135.7 ms during 4th ITI and shortened to 619.6±58.1 ms by 10th ITI.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 document dynamic changes in call characteristics with appropriate statistical tests. The failure to reach significance for 44-kHz frequency changes (C55) is appropriately reported. The temporal patterns are consistent with the proposed arousal hypothesis, though alternative explanations exist.

results.result: The amplitude of 44-kHz calls remained stable throughout training, while 22-kHz call amplitude decreased significantly in the second half (p<0.0001). After correcting for microphone angle-dependent attenuation (+10 dB for 44-kHz), 44-kHz calls were significantly louder than 22-kHz calls during 6th-10th ITI (p=0.0007-0.0097).
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 provide amplitude analysis with important technical correction for hardware limitations. The angle-dependent attenuation correction (C64) is crucial but relies on approximations (45° angle, conservative 10 dB estimate). The reversal of findings after correction highlights the importance of this adjustment, though uncertainty in the correction magnitude limits precision.

results.result: Freezing during 44-kHz call emission was significantly higher than baseline (p=0.0003) and no-call periods (p=0.0353), but not significantly different from freezing during 22-kHz calls (9.9 percentage points higher, p=0.1907). High-resolution analysis of individual calls (≥150 ms and ≥500 ms) showed no significant differences in freezing between 44-kHz and 22-kHz vocalizations.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 demonstrate association between 44-kHz calls and freezing behavior with appropriate statistical analyses at multiple temporal resolutions. The lack of significant difference from 22-kHz calls (C68-C70) is important for interpretation. However, the 10-s bin analysis (C65-C68) may not capture moment-to-moment relationships as well as the frame-by-frame analysis (C69-C70).

results.result: Long 22-kHz and 44-kHz vocalizations show a stable ~1.5 (3:2) frequency ratio within individual rats (1.48±0.02 for transitions, 1.53±0.03 for step up, 1.59±0.02 for step down calls), suggesting they constitute a supertype group of 'long 22/44-kHz vocalizations'. This ratio corresponds to a perfect fifth in music theory and has been observed across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C83 propose an interesting relationship with quantitative support from multiple call types. The consistency of the ratio across different analyses strengthens the finding. However, the proposal of a 'supertype group' (C76) is interpretive and the functional significance of the musical interval analogy (C81-C83), while intriguing, remains speculative.

results.result: Two independent clustering methods confirmed 44-kHz calls as a separable vocalization type: DBSCAN separated 44-kHz from other vocalizations based on frequency and duration, while k-means with UMAP sorted 44-kHz subtypes into topologically-separate groups, with flat 44-kHz calls consistently clustering separately from 22-kHz calls.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C84-C86 provide computational validation using complementary approaches. The DBSCAN silhouette coefficient of 0.198 is relatively low, suggesting moderate cluster quality, but the convergence of two methods strengthens the conclusion. The consistent separation of flat 44-kHz from 22-kHz calls (C86) is particularly important for establishing distinctiveness.

results.result: Transition probability analysis showed that 44-kHz calls form sequential bouts: the probability of a 44-kHz call following another 44-kHz call was 83.1% (86.5% within bouts), similar to 22-kHz calls (94.4%, 96.3% within bouts).
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 demonstrate temporal clustering with clear quantitative results. The bout analysis using <320 ms gaps is based on established criteria (Wöhr et al., 2005). The high transition probabilities support the interpretation that these calls form coherent groups, though they are somewhat lower than for 22-kHz calls.

results.result: Playback experiments showed that rats' heart rate responses to 44-kHz calls were similar to aversive 22-kHz calls (both decreased) rather than appetitive 50-kHz calls (increased), despite 44-kHz calls occupying the frequency band of 50-kHz vocalizations. Other responses (vocalization number, duration, locomotion) were intermediate between 22-kHz and 50-kHz playback responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C97, C126-C127 provide functional validation through playback experiments with multiple behavioral and physiological measures. The dissociation between frequency band and behavioral response (C127) challenges simple frequency-based models. However, potential carry-over effects are acknowledged, and the intermediate responses complicate interpretation of the calls' valence.

results.result: The authors propose that 44-kHz vocalizations communicate an increased negative emotional state associated with heightened arousal during prolonged fear conditioning, supported by: (1) emission during prolonged aversive stimulation, (2) association with freezing, (3) partial replacement of 22-kHz calls, (4) mixed call elements, (5) comparable or higher amplitude than 22-kHz calls despite higher energy costs, and (6) stable amplitude over trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C110, C124 present an interpretive framework with supporting observations. While the evidence is consistent with increased arousal (C99), the authors acknowledge multiple alternative explanations (fatigue, despair, etc.) cannot be definitively ruled out. The interpretation as 'increased negative emotional state' (C100) is reasonable but speculative, as direct measures of emotional state are not available.

results.result: 22-kHz call amplitude decreased significantly during fear conditioning training, potentially due to fatigue or despair, a finding replicated by Gonzalez-Palomares et al., 2023.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 document amplitude changes with statistical support and independent replication. However, the mechanistic interpretation (C112) is speculative, and the authors appropriately present it as such. The replication (C113) strengthens confidence in the observation.

results.result: Training with multiple shocks (5-10) produces qualitatively different fear memories than 1-2 shocks, characterized by augmented freezing, resistance to extinction and reconsolidation blockade, molecular changes in the amygdala, and correlation with stress hormones. Rats in the current study receiving 6-10 shocks showed higher freezing than those receiving 1 shock.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C123 provide context from prior literature with appropriate citations and confirm the expected behavioral pattern in the current study. This establishes that the experimental conditions producing 44-kHz calls are associated with intense fear memories, supporting the interpretation. However, these are primarily literature claims rather than novel findings.

results.result: Long, frequency-stable high-pitch vocalizations have been reported previously (e.g., following cholinergic stimulation or higher shock-dose conditioning) but were not systematically characterized. The authors suggest 44-kHz calls were overlooked due to: (1) restriction to canonical call types with sharp frequency borders, (2) limited frequency range of older equipment, and (3) lower emission rates than 22-kHz calls.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C134 provide reasonable explanations for why these calls were not previously characterized, with appropriate citations. The explanations are plausible and supported by methodological details from cited studies. However, the claim that these calls have 'not yet been described' (C30, C131) may be overstated given prior observations, though the systematic characterization is indeed novel.

results.result: The authors conclude that 44-kHz vocalizations represent a separate and behaviorally relevant group of rat ultrasonic calls, expanding the known vocal repertoire, and recommend that researchers be aware of their presence and not rely solely on automated frequency-based detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C138 represent the main conclusions, which are supported by the convergent evidence from acoustic characterization, clustering analyses, behavioral associations, and playback experiments. The recommendation for methodological awareness (C137-C138) is appropriate given the findings. However, the authors appropriately note that further confirmation and replication are needed.

results.result: The manuscript reviews established knowledge about rat ultrasonic vocalizations: rats communicate emotional states through 22-kHz calls (long, <32 kHz, aversive) and 50-kHz calls (short, >32 kHz, appetitive), with the relationship between pitch and emotional state noted since Darwin. High-pitch, long, monotonous calls had not been systematically described prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C30 accurately summarize established knowledge with appropriate citations. These provide necessary context for the novel findings. The claim of novelty (C30) is supported by the literature review, though some prior observations exist (acknowledged in C128-C131).

results.result: 44-kHz and 22-kHz calls share key characteristics: both are emitted in aversive situations, are long (usually >300 ms), and are frequency-unmodulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 summarize shared characteristics that support the proposed relationship between call types. These observations are well-documented in the results and consistent with the supertype proposal (C76).

results.result: The manuscript cites general principles: frequency typically increases with arousal in animal vocalizations, producing higher-pitched calls requires more energy and muscle activity, and rat vocalizations can alter emotional states in conspecifics via playback.
results.evaluation: Claims C98, C106, C108, C125 cite established principles with appropriate references that provide theoretical context for interpreting the findings. These are accurately represented literature claims.

results.result: The authors report that 44-kHz ultrasonic vocalizations occur in male Wistar and SHR rats during prolonged fear conditioning. Specifically, 53 of 84 Wistar rats (63%) and 6 of 49 SHR (12%) displayed these calls, with 10,445 total 44-kHz calls identified constituting 7.5% of all calls during fear conditioning experiments. Among rats undergoing 10-trial conditioning, 69.6% (32/46) emitted 44-kHz calls.
results.evaluation: The editor states the study 'investigated the appearance of ultrasonic vocalizations around 44 kHz that occurs in response to prolonged fear conditioning' and describes evidence as 'solid.' The anonymous reviewer acknowledges the authors 'observed so-called "44-kHz" calls in a substantial number of subjects exposed to 10 tone-shock pairings,' though notes 'call emission rate was low.' Both reviewers accept the basic observation of these vocalizations without challenging their existence.

results.result: The authors characterize 44-kHz vocalizations as long (>150 ms), generally at constant frequency within 35-50 kHz range, with spectrographic similarity to 22-kHz calls. They report peak frequency range of 32.2-51.5 kHz (95% of cases) with average of 42.1 kHz, and validation showing 99.8% correct classification using criteria of >32 kHz peak frequency and >150 ms duration.
results.evaluation: The editor describes this as a 'valuable study' with 'solid' evidence. The anonymous reviewer acknowledges the 'detailed spectrographic analysis of a substantial data set' as a strength and does not challenge the acoustic characterization. The reviewers accept the descriptive acoustic parameters without raising methodological concerns.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that 44-kHz calls constitute a separable vocalization type using two clustering methods: DBSCAN algorithm based on peak frequency and duration separated 44-kHz from other vocalizations, and k-means with UMAP sorted 44-kHz subtypes into topologically-separate groups, with flat 44-kHz calls consistently clustering separately from 22-kHz calls.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly identifies 'detailed spectrographic analysis' as a strength and does not challenge the clustering methodology or conclusions. The editor's assessment of 'solid' evidence implicitly supports these analytical approaches. No concerns are raised about the separability claims.

results.result: The authors report temporal dynamics showing 44-kHz calls were less frequent after the first trial (1.2±0.4%), increased particularly after the 5th trial (8.8±2.8%), peaked at the 9th trial (19.4±5.5%), and were emitted predominantly in the second half of training (5th-10th ITI), while 22-kHz calls peaked earlier (3rd ITI). More 44-kHz vocalizations occurred during training than testing (3.63±0.99 vs 0.23±0.13 calls/min, p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer notes the observation of 44-kHz calls 'in response to prolonged fear conditioning' without challenging the temporal pattern. The editor's assessment of 'solid' evidence encompasses these temporal dynamics. The specific claim about emission rates (around 7.5% according to result text, up to 19.4% in some trials) is acknowledged by the reviewer without dispute.

results.result: The authors report that 44-kHz calls are associated with freezing behavior during fear conditioning. Freezing during bins with 44-kHz calls was higher than baseline (p=0.0003) and higher than during bins with no vocalizations (p=0.0353), though 9.9 percentage points higher than during 22-kHz calls, this difference was not significant (p=0.1907). High-resolution analysis showed no difference in freezing during emission of 44-kHz vs 22-kHz vocalizations for calls ≥150 ms or ≥500 ms.
results.evaluation: Neither reviewer challenges the freezing behavior data or its association with 44-kHz calls. The editor's assessment of 'solid' evidence and the anonymous reviewer's acknowledgment of 'detailed spectrographic analysis' combined with behavioral measures implicitly support these findings. No methodological concerns are raised about the freezing measurements.

results.result: The authors classify 44-kHz vocalizations into five subtypes (flat, step up, step down, insert, and complex) based on composition of call elements. Some 44-kHz vocalizations contain both 22-kHz-like and 44-kHz-like elements, with some elements in step up, step down, insert and complex subtypes at lower frequencies typical of 22-kHz vocalizations, and vice versa.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer's acknowledgment of 'detailed spectrographic analysis' as a strength encompasses this subtype classification. Neither reviewer challenges the categorization scheme or the observation of mixed-frequency elements. The editor's assessment of 'solid' evidence supports these descriptive findings.

results.result: The authors report frequency and duration changes over training: 22-kHz call frequencies gradually rose from 24.5±0.1 to 27.9±0.4 kHz (p<0.0001), while 44-kHz frequencies appeared to rise from 37.8±2.1 to 39.6±1.3 kHz but without statistical significance (p=0.0977). Long 22-kHz calls shortened during first four ITI from 969.6±43.1 to 794.6±39.8 ms (p<0.0001), while 44-kHz calls were longest at 4th ITI (775.0±135.7 ms) and shortened to 619.6±58.1 ms by 10th ITI (p=0.0234).
results.evaluation: Neither reviewer challenges these temporal dynamics of acoustic parameters. The editor's assessment of 'solid' evidence and the anonymous reviewer's recognition of 'detailed spectrographic analysis' support these quantitative findings. The authors' acknowledgment of non-significant trends for 44-kHz frequency changes demonstrates appropriate statistical interpretation.

results.result: The authors report amplitude patterns showing 44-kHz vocalization mean power remained stable throughout 10-trial sessions, while 22-kHz calls were louder in the first half (1st-5th ITI) than second half (6th-10th ITI, p<0.0001) with significant decrease over training (p=0.0083). After adjusting for angle-dependent hardware attenuation, 44-kHz calls were significantly louder than 22-kHz calls during 6th-10th ITI (p=0.0007-0.0097), with 44-kHz mean power comparable to or higher than 22-kHz calls.
results.evaluation: Neither reviewer challenges the amplitude measurements or the technical correction for hardware attenuation. The anonymous reviewer's acknowledgment of 'detailed spectrographic analysis' encompasses these acoustic measurements. The editor's assessment of 'solid' evidence supports these findings without raising methodological concerns.

results.result: The authors propose that long 22-kHz and 44-kHz vocalizations constitute a supertype group of 'long unmodulated aversive calls' based on shared characteristics: both emitted in aversive situations, both long (usually >300 ms) and frequency-unmodulated. They report a stable ~1.5 frequency ratio between 22-kHz and 44-kHz vocalizations within individual rats (1.48±0.02 for transitions, 1.53±0.03 for step up, 1.59±0.02 for step down calls).
results.evaluation: Neither reviewer challenges this proposed classification or the frequency ratio observations. The editor's assessment of 'solid' evidence and the anonymous reviewer's acknowledgment of detailed analysis support these interpretive findings. The mathematical relationship between call types is presented as data-driven observation rather than speculation.

results.result: The authors report that 44-kHz calls form temporal bouts with high transition probabilities: the most probable call following a 44-kHz vocalization was another 44-kHz call (83.1%), increasing to 86.5% when analysis was limited to bouts (<320 ms gaps). Similarly, 22-kHz calls showed 94.4% probability of being followed by another 22-kHz call (96.3% in bouts). Most 44-kHz calls appeared next to each other forming uniform groups.
results.evaluation: Neither reviewer challenges the bout structure or transition probability analysis. The anonymous reviewer's acknowledgment of 'detailed spectrographic analysis' encompasses these sequential patterns. The editor's assessment of 'solid' evidence supports these findings about temporal organization of vocalizations.

results.result: The authors report playback experiment results showing rats' responses to 44-kHz calls were either similar to aversive 22-kHz calls (heart rate decreased for both 22-kHz and 44-kHz, increased for 50-kHz) or intermediate between aversive and appetitive calls (number of vocalizations emitted was highest for 50-kHz, intermediate for 44-kHz, lowest for 22-kHz; duration of emitted 50-kHz calls was intermediate for 44-kHz playback). Similar intermediate patterns were observed for distance traveled and time spent near speaker.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly acknowledges the authors 'performed playback experiments and concluded that "the responses to 44-kHz aversive calls presented from the speaker were either similar to 22-kHz vocalizations or in-between responses to 22-kHz and 50-kHz playbacks"' without challenging these findings. The editor's assessment of 'solid' evidence encompasses the playback results. The combination of playback with spectrographic analysis is noted as a strength.

results.result: The authors propose that prolonged fear conditioning increased arousal with no change in valence, and that 44-kHz vocalizations communicate an increased negative emotional state associated with increased stress and training regimes forming robust memories. They argue this is supported by multiple lines of evidence including the aversive context, temporal patterns, association with freezing, and playback responses.
results.evaluation: The editor describes the study as investigating 'distress-related ultrasonic vocalizations,' accepting the aversive interpretation. The anonymous reviewer does not challenge the interpretation that these are aversive calls. While this is interpretive rather than directly measured, both reviewers implicitly accept the authors' framework linking 44-kHz calls to negative emotional states without raising alternative interpretations.

results.result: The authors claim that high-pitch (>32 kHz), long and monotonous ultrasonic vocalizations have not been systematically defined, described, or demonstrated as a separate vocalization type prior to this study, though similar calls have been reported in specific contexts (cholinergic stimulation, higher shock-dose conditioning). They argue 44-kHz calls were likely omitted in previous studies due to restricted analyses with sharp frequency borders, frequency 'safety gaps,' and limited detector ranges (up to 40 kHz), and that 44-kHz vocalizations represent a separate and behaviorally relevant group.
results.evaluation: The editor describes this as a 'valuable study' that 'may be of interest to some researchers also investigating distress-related ultrasonic vocalizations,' implicitly accepting the novelty claim. The anonymous reviewer does not challenge the novelty assertion and acknowledges the 'detailed spectrographic analysis' without suggesting these calls were already well-characterized. Neither reviewer disputes that this represents a systematic characterization of a previously under-recognized call type.

results.result: The authors cite Gonzalez-Palomares et al., 2023 as describing 44-kHz vocalizations following prolonged (10-trial) odor fear conditioning, with calls observed predominantly during late ITI (8th-10th) after shock presentations, complementing the current results. They also cite this work as observing reduction in amplitude of 22-kHz calls during 10-trial training.
results.evaluation: Neither reviewer challenges these citations or suggests they undermine the novelty of the current work. The authors present this as complementary evidence published during review, and reviewers accept this contextualization. The editor's assessment that the study 'may be of interest to some researchers' acknowledges the emerging literature without diminishing the contribution.

results.result: The authors contextualize their findings within established fear conditioning literature, citing that training with 5-10 shocks produces qualitatively different fear memory than 1-2 shocks, resulting in augmented freezing that reflects more intense, extinction-resistant, reconsolidation-resistant memories with specific molecular signatures (NR2B downregulation, elevated amyloid-beta, noradrenaline-locus coeruleus activation, network connectivity changes). They report their 6- and 10-trial trained rats showed higher freezing than 1-trial rats, and that higher freezing correlates with increased corticosterone.
results.evaluation: Neither reviewer challenges this contextualization or the cited literature. The anonymous reviewer acknowledges the use of 'foot-shocks of relatively high intensity, i.e. 1 mA' and 'prolonged fear conditioning' without disputing the characterization of this as an intensified paradigm. The editor's description of 'distress-related' vocalizations aligns with this framework. The comparative freezing data is not challenged.

comparisons.comparison: Both support the basic observation of 44-kHz vocalizations during fear conditioning (C1, C2, C31-C33). OpenEval provides detailed quantitative assessment with sample sizes and p-values, while peer reviewers accept the observation as 'solid' evidence despite noting low emission rates.

Both support the acoustic characterization (C3-C6, C35-C39). OpenEval notes the 99.8% classification accuracy and large sample size while acknowledging potential circularity in threshold setting. Peer reviewers describe the 'detailed spectrographic analysis' as a strength without raising methodological concerns.

Both support the structural heterogeneity and subtype classification (C7, C71, C74-C75). OpenEval notes the lack of inter-rater reliability reporting for manual sorting, while peer reviewers accept the categorization as part of the 'detailed spectrographic analysis' strength.

Both support the temporal dynamics and progressive emergence pattern (C40-C45). OpenEval provides detailed quantitative assessment noting high individual variability, while peer reviewers acknowledge the observation in response to prolonged conditioning without challenging the temporal patterns.

Both support the context-specificity with independent replication (C51-C53). OpenEval emphasizes the convergent evidence from different laboratories and paradigms, while peer reviewers accept these citations as complementary evidence without challenging the contextualization.

Both support the dynamic changes in call characteristics (C54-C58). OpenEval notes the appropriate reporting of non-significant findings for 44-kHz frequency changes, while peer reviewers accept these temporal dynamics without methodological concerns.

Both support the amplitude analysis with technical corrections (C59-C64). OpenEval highlights the importance of the angle-dependent attenuation correction while noting uncertainty in correction magnitude, while peer reviewers accept the amplitude measurements without raising concerns about the technical adjustments.

Both support the association between 44-kHz calls and freezing behavior (C65-C70). OpenEval notes the multiple temporal resolutions and lack of significant difference from 22-kHz calls, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the behavioral measures as part of the 'solid' evidence.

Both support the frequency ratio relationship and 'supertype group' proposal (C76-C80, C72-C73). OpenEval notes the consistency across analyses but acknowledges the musical interval analogy remains speculative, while peer reviewers accept the classification without challenging the interpretive framework.

Both support the computational validation using clustering approaches (C8, C84-C86). OpenEval notes the relatively low silhouette coefficient (0.198) but emphasizes convergence of methods, while peer reviewers accept the clustering methodology as part of the detailed analysis strength.

Both support the temporal clustering and bout structure analysis (C87-C89). OpenEval notes the use of established criteria and somewhat lower transition probabilities compared to 22-kHz calls, while peer reviewers accept the sequential pattern findings without challenge.

Both support the playback experiment findings (C90-C97, C126-C127). OpenEval notes the dissociation between frequency band and behavioral response while acknowledging potential carry-over effects, while peer reviewers explicitly quote the intermediate response findings without challenging the interpretation.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN while peer reviewers SUPPORT the arousal/negative emotional state interpretation (C99-C100, C124). OpenEval emphasizes multiple alternative explanations cannot be ruled out and direct measures are lacking, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the aversive framework without raising alternative interpretations.

Both support the amplitude changes with replication (C111-C113). OpenEval notes the mechanistic interpretation is speculative but appropriately presented, while peer reviewers accept the amplitude measurements as part of the detailed acoustic analysis.

Both support the contextualization from prior literature (C114-C123). OpenEval notes these are primarily literature claims rather than novel findings, while peer reviewers accept the characterization of intensified paradigm and comparative freezing data without dispute.

Both support the explanations for why these calls were not previously characterized (C128-C133, C135-C136). OpenEval suggests the novelty claim may be overstated given prior observations, while peer reviewers accept the novelty assertion and describe the work as 'valuable' without challenging the systematic characterization claim.

Both support the main conclusions and methodological recommendations (C135-C138). OpenEval notes the convergent evidence while emphasizing need for further confirmation, while peer reviewers describe the study as 'valuable' and accept the contribution to the field.

OpenEval evaluates the established knowledge summary (C14-C30) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this background literature review section.

Both support the shared characteristics between call types (C72-C73). OpenEval notes these observations support the supertype proposal, while peer reviewers accept these as part of the frequency ratio relationship without separate evaluation.

OpenEval evaluates the theoretical context citations (C98, C106, C108, C125) as SUPPORTED and accurately represented. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these theoretical framework citations.
